html:
Electrochemistry is the chemistry of electrons that travel through a wire instead of jumping between atoms.

The paper carries about one question from this chapter (our estimate from the MEC topic list), and it comes in three shapes: a Faraday's-law calculation with 96 500 C in it, a cell-potential subtraction, or a fact about a named cell (SHE, calomel, lead–acid, fuel cell) with one word changed.

The two ideas that decide most marks are that oxidation is always at the anode in both kinds of cell, and that E° is an intensive property — doubling a half-reaction does not double the voltage.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Electrolytic cell: electrical → chemical, anode positive, cathode negative. Galvanic cell: chemical → electrical, anode negative, cathode positive. Oxidation at the anode in both.
  • Faraday's first law m = ZIt with Z = E/96500; second law m_1/m_2 = E_1/E_2; one faraday (96 500 C) deposits one gram equivalent.
  • Standard electrode potential is a reduction potential, measured against the SHE, which is fixed at 0.00 V (1 M H⁺, 1 atm H₂, 298 K, Pt).
  • Calomel electrode: a secondary reference, Hg₂Cl₂/Hg in KCl, 0.24 V when saturated.
  • The electrochemical series gives reactivity, displacement, cell emf and the products of electrolysis.
  • E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}; positive means spontaneous. E^\circ is intensive.
  • Nernst: E = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q at 298 K; \Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ.
  • Primary (dry cell, 1.5 V), secondary (lead–acid 2 V per cell, lithium-ion) and fuel cells (H₂–O₂, water is the only product); rusting is an electrochemical cell.

10.1 Electrolytic cells and the qualitative and quantitative laws of electrolysis

The electrolytic cell

Electrolysis and electrolytic cell

Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by the passage of a direct electric current. The apparatus — two electrodes dipping into the electrolyte, connected to a source of direct current — is an electrolytic cell.

It converts electrical energy into chemical energy.

  • The anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply. Oxidation happens there: anions lose electrons.
  • The cathode is the electrode connected to the negative terminal. Reduction happens there: cations gain electrons.
  • In the external circuit electrons travel from the anode to the positive terminal of the battery, and from its negative terminal to the cathode. Inside the electrolyte the current is carried by ions, not electrons.
  • The electrolyte must be an ionic conductor — a molten salt, or a solution of an acid, base or salt. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct.

Products of electrolysis — the qualitative laws

What appears at the electrodes depends on three things: the electrolyte, the material of the electrodes and the concentration. The rules of preferential discharge are:

  • At the cathode, the ion that is more easily reduced — the one with the higher (more positive) standard reduction potential — is discharged first. In aqueous solution Cu²⁺, Ag⁺ and H⁺ compete; Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ are never discharged from water, because hydrogen is liberated instead.
  • At the anode, the species more easily oxidised is discharged. With inert electrodes in water, OH⁻/H₂O is oxidised to O₂ unless a concentrated halide is present, when Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂ appears.
Electrolyte Electrodes At cathode At anode
Molten NaCl inert Na Cl₂
Aqueous NaCl (concentrated brine) inert H₂ Cl₂
Dilute NaCl solution inert H₂ O₂
Aqueous CuSO₄ platinum (inert) Cu O₂
Aqueous CuSO₄ copper Cu (pure) Cu dissolves
Acidified water platinum H₂ O₂
Molten Al₂O₃ in cryolite carbon Al O₂ (which burns the carbon to CO₂)

The copper-refining case is the important exception: with copper electrodes, copper dissolves at the anode and is deposited at the cathode, so the concentration of CuSO₄ stays constant and impure copper is refined.

Anode is not always the positive electrode

In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive; in a galvanic cell the anode is negative. What never changes is that oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

A question that says "oxidation occurs at the positive electrode" is wrong for a galvanic cell, and "at the cathode" is wrong for both.

Faraday's first law

Faraday's first law of electrolysis

The mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte: m \propto Q, or m = ZQ = ZIt, where I is the current in amperes, t the time in seconds and Z the electrochemical equivalent — the mass deposited by one coulomb.

m = ZIt \qquad Z = \frac{E}{96500}

E is the equivalent weight in g equiv⁻¹, equal to the molar mass divided by the number of electrons in the half-reaction (E = M/n). The constant 96 500 C is one faraday (F), the charge on one mole of electrons.

F = N_A \times e = (6.02 \times 10^{23})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \approx 96\,500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}

Faraday's second law

Faraday's second law of electrolysis

When the same quantity of electricity is passed through several electrolytes in series, the masses of the substances deposited are proportional to their equivalent weights: \frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{E_1}{E_2}.

Equivalently, one faraday deposits one gram equivalent of any substance.

Substance Half-reaction n E = M/n Mass from 96 500 C
Ag Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag 1 108 108 g
Cu Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu 2 31.75 31.75 g
Al Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al 3 9 9 g
H₂ 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ 2 1 1 g (11.2 L at STP)
O₂ 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ 4 8 8 g (5.6 L at STP)
Cl₂ 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ 2 35.5 35.5 g (11.2 L at STP)
Faraday's first law with 96 500 C

Problem. A current of 9.65 A is passed through silver nitrate solution for 100 s. Find the mass of silver deposited (Ag = 108).

Solution. Q = It = 9.65 \times 100 = 965 C. Moles of electrons = \frac{965}{96\,500} = 0.010 mol.

Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, so 0.010 mol of Ag is deposited: m = 0.010 \times 108 = \mathbf{1.08} g. By the formula: Z = \frac{108}{96\,500} = 1.119 \times 10^{-3} g C⁻¹, and m = 1.119 \times 10^{-3} \times 965 = 1.08 g.

Charge needed for a stated mass

Problem. What charge is needed to deposit 1.0 g of copper from copper sulphate solution? How long will it take at 1.0 A? (Cu = 63.5)

Solution. Moles of Cu = 1.0/63.5 = 0.0157 mol. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 mol of electrons per mole of copper, so n(e^-) = 0.0315 mol. Q = 0.0315 \times 96\,500 = \mathbf{3040} C (about 3.0 × 10³ C). t = Q/I = 3040/1.0 = \mathbf{3040} s ≈ 51 min.

Volumes of gases from a charge

Problem. 965 C is passed through acidified water between platinum electrodes. What volume of hydrogen and of oxygen, at STP, is liberated?

Solution. 965 C = 0.010 mol of electrons. Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, so H₂ = 0.010/2 = 0.005 mol = 0.005 \times 22\,400 = 112 mL. Anode: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so O₂ = 0.010/4 = 0.0025 mol = 56 mL. The volumes are in the 2 : 1 ratio the formula of water demands.

The 96 500 arithmetic in one line

Convert everything to moles of electrons first: n(e^-) = \frac{It}{96\,500}. Then divide by the number of electrons in the half-reaction to get moles of substance, and multiply by the molar mass.

Nearly every Faraday question falls to this single chain, and it avoids the equivalent-weight formula going upside down.

10.2 Standard electrode potential, the SHE and the calomel electrode, and the electrochemical series

Electrode potential

When a metal is dipped into a solution of its own ions, two opposing processes start: metal atoms leave the lattice as ions (oxidation), and ions from solution deposit on the metal (reduction).

A separation of charge builds up until the two rates balance, leaving the metal with a definite potential relative to the solution — its electrode potential.

Standard electrode potential

The standard electrode potential E^\circ of a half-cell is the potential of that half-cell measured against the standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K, with every ion at 1 mol L⁻¹ (or 1 bar for gases).

By IUPAC convention it is quoted as a reduction potential: it refers to the half-reaction written as a reduction, M^{n+} + ne^- \rightarrow M.

A single electrode potential cannot be measured on its own — only a difference between two electrodes can. So one electrode is chosen as the zero and everything is quoted against it.

The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)

The SHE is a platinum plate coated with finely divided platinum black, dipping into 1 M H⁺ (strictly, unit activity) with hydrogen gas bubbled over it at 1 atm and 298 K.

2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 \qquad E^\circ = 0.00\ \text{V (by definition)}

  • Platinum black is used because it adsorbs hydrogen and catalyses the electrode reaction; platinum itself does not take part.
  • To measure the potential of another electrode, it is paired with the SHE and the reading of the voltmeter is the required potential — sign included.
  • If the unknown electrode is the cathode, the reading is its reduction potential; if it is the anode, the reading is the negative of that.
Feature Standard hydrogen electrode Calomel electrode
Composition Pt black, 1 M H⁺, H₂ at 1 atm Hg over Hg₂Cl₂ paste in KCl solution
Electrode reaction 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ Hg₂Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Hg + 2Cl⁻
Potential at 25 °C 0.00 V by definition 0.28 V (1 M KCl), 0.24 V (saturated)
Role primary reference secondary reference
Practical drawback needs a constant supply of pure H₂; fragile; hard to set up —

The calomel electrode

A calomel electrode is mercury in contact with a paste of mercury(I) chloride (calomel, Hg₂Cl₂) and potassium chloride solution, with a platinum wire for contact.

Hg_2Cl_2(s) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2Hg(l) + 2Cl^-(aq)

Its potential depends on the chloride concentration, because Cl⁻ appears in the half-reaction. The saturated calomel electrode (SCE) is the laboratory standard: 0.2415 V at 25 °C.

It is preferred to the SHE because it is compact, portable, needs no hydrogen gas and gives a steady, reproducible potential — which is why it is called a secondary reference electrode.

Reference electrodes are not zero

Only the SHE is defined as 0.00 V. A calomel electrode has a real potential of about +0.24 V, so a reading taken against it must be corrected before it is quoted against the SHE. Options that call calomel "the zero of the scale" are wrong.

The electrochemical series

Arranging the standard reduction potentials in order gives the electrochemical series (activity series). The values below are the ones the paper uses.

Half-reaction (reduction) E^\circ (V) Half-reaction (reduction) E^\circ (V)
F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻ +2.87 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ 0.00
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O +1.51 Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb −0.13
Au³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Au +1.50 Sn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Sn −0.14
Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ +1.36 Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni −0.25
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O +1.33 Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe −0.44
O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O +1.23 Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn −0.76
Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻ +1.09 Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al −1.66
Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag +0.80 Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg −2.37
Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ +0.77 Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na −2.71
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu +0.34 K⁺ + e⁻ → K −2.93
I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻ +0.54 Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li −3.05

The four uses of the series — every one of them is examinable.

  1. Reactivity and reducing strength. The lower (more negative) the E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the stronger its reducing power: K > Na > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb

    H > Cu > Ag > Au. Metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from dilute acids; copper, silver and gold do not.

  2. Displacement reactions. A metal higher in the series displaces a metal lower down from a solution of its salt: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. The reverse never happens spontaneously. The same rule predicts halogen displacement: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.
  3. Cell emf. E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}. A positive value means the reaction as written is spontaneous.
  4. Predicting the products of electrolysis. At the cathode, the ion with the higher E^\circ is discharged; at the anode, the species with the lower E^\circ is oxidised. This is why copper, not hydrogen, is deposited from CuSO₄ solution, and why sodium is never obtained from aqueous NaCl.
Two sentences that answer half the questions

"Higher E^\circ wins the electrons" — that is the cathode. "Lower E^\circ loses them" — that is the anode. Everything else (displacement, corrosion, electrolysis products) is this one rule applied twice.

10.3 Galvanic cells and their standard emf; primary, secondary and hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

The galvanic (voltaic) cell

Galvanic cell

A galvanic cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.

The two half-reactions are carried out in separate compartments joined by a salt bridge, so that the electrons must travel through an external wire to get from the reducing agent to the oxidising agent.

In the Daniell cell, zinc is dipped into ZnSO₄ and copper into CuSO₄.

  • Anode (negative): zinc is oxidised, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Electrons leave the cell here.
  • Cathode (positive): copper ions are reduced, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
  • Salt bridge: a tube of KCl or KNO₃ in agar. It lets ions move — cations towards the cathode compartment, anions towards the anode — so that both solutions stay electrically neutral. Without it the cell stops after a few seconds.

Cell notation writes the same cell on one line:

\text{Zn(s)} \mid \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) \parallel \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \mid \text{Cu(s)}

  • The anode is written on the left and the cathode on the right.
  • A single bar | is a phase boundary; the double bar || is the salt bridge.
  • By convention the cell emf is the potential of the right-hand electrode minus that of the left-hand one, which is why the anode must be on the left for a positive reading.

Standard emf of the cell

E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = E^\circ_{\text{right}} - E^\circ_{\text{left}}

For the Daniell cell: E^\circ = (+0.34) - (-0.76) = \mathbf{1.10} V.

  • A positive E^\circ_{\text{cell}} means the cell reaction as written is spontaneous and the cell delivers current.
  • A negative value means the reaction runs the other way; the cell as written is electrolytic, not galvanic.
  • E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0 means the cell is dead — equilibrium has been reached.
E° is intensive — doubling a half-reaction changes nothing

E^\circ is a potential difference, an intensive property, like temperature.

Multiplying the coefficients of a half-reaction by 2 doubles \Delta G^\circ and doubles the number of electrons n, but leaves E^\circ unchanged, because \Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ and both \Delta G^\circ and n double.

Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn has E^\circ = -0.76 V; so does 2Zn²⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2Zn. Only when you reverse a half-reaction does the sign flip. This is the single most common wrong key in electrochemistry papers.

Free energy and the equilibrium constant. The electrical work a cell can do is the decrease in free energy:

\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ

with n the number of moles of electrons transferred and F = 96\,500 C mol⁻¹. For the Daniell cell, n = 2 and E^\circ = 1.10 V: \Delta G^\circ = -2(96\,500)(1.10) = -2.12 \times 10^5 J mol⁻¹ = −212 kJ mol⁻¹.

At equilibrium E = 0 and \Delta G = 0, so E^\circ = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K at 298 K.

The Nernst equation

Real cells do not run at 1 M. The emf depends on concentration:

E = E^\circ - \frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q \quad (298\ \text{K})

where Q is the reaction quotient in the same form as an equilibrium constant.

  • If the products are at low concentration (Q < 1), E > E^\circ.
  • If the reactants are at low concentration (Q > 1), E < E^\circ.
  • As the cell discharges, Q rises and E falls until Q = K and E = 0: the cell is flat.
Nernst equation for a dilute half-cell

Problem. Find the emf at 298 K of Zn | Zn²⁺(0.01 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu, given E^\circ = 1.10 V.

Solution. The cell reaction is Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, so Q = [\text{Zn}^{2+}]/[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 0.01/1 = 0.01 and n = 2. E = 1.10 - \frac{0.059}{2}\log(0.01) = 1.10 - 0.0295(-2) = 1.10 + 0.059 = \mathbf{1.16} V. Diluting the anode compartment makes the cell stronger, because the zinc has more room to dissolve.

Primary, secondary and fuel cells

Cell Anode Cathode Electrolyte emf Rechargeable
Leclanché dry cell (primary) zinc can MnO₂ + carbon rod NH₄Cl + ZnCl₂ paste 1.5 V no
Alkaline cell (primary) zinc powder MnO₂ KOH 1.5 V no
Lead–acid accumulator (secondary) Pb PbO₂ dilute H₂SO₄ 2 V per cell yes
Lithium-ion (secondary) graphite (LiC₆) LiCoO₂ Li salt in organic solvent 3.7 V yes
H₂–O₂ fuel cell porous carbon with H₂ porous carbon with O₂ KOH or polymer membrane 1.23 V continuous

The dry cell. The zinc container is itself the anode; a central carbon rod with MnO₂ and graphite powder is the cathode; the paste of NH₄Cl and ZnCl₂ is the electrolyte.

  • Anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
  • Cathode: 2MnO₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn₂O₃ + H₂O
  • Overall: Zn + 2MnO₂ + 2NH₄⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Mn₂O₃ + 2NH₃ + H₂O

The zinc can is gradually eaten away, which is why an old dry cell leaks. It cannot be recharged because the electrode reactions are not easily reversed.

The lead–acid accumulator. Six cells in series give the familiar 12 V car battery.

  • Anode: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻
  • Cathode: PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
  • Overall: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

Both electrodes become lead(II) sulphate on discharge, and the sulphuric acid is diluted — which is why the density of the electrolyte is used to test the state of charge. Recharging reverses both half-reactions exactly.

The hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell. Hydrogen is fed to the anode and oxygen to the cathode of porous carbon electrodes; the only product is water.

  • Anode (alkaline): 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻
  • Cathode (alkaline): O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
  • Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

Its efficiency is about 70 %, far above the 30–40 % of a heat engine, because it is not limited by the Carnot cycle. Fuel cells powered the Apollo spacecraft and are the model for hydrogen vehicles.

Corrosion as an electrochemical cell

Rusting is not a simple combination of iron with oxygen; it needs both oxygen and water, and it happens through tiny short-circuited galvanic cells on the metal surface.

  1. At anodic patches (where the metal is strained or less protected), iron dissolves: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.
  2. The electrons travel through the metal to cathodic patches, where dissolved oxygen is reduced: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
  3. The ions meet and precipitate iron(II) hydroxide, which is oxidised further by air to hydrated iron(III) oxide — rust, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

The water film acts as the electrolyte and the metal itself is the wire, so iron is the anode and is consumed. Anything that makes iron the cathode protects it:

Method How it works
Galvanising (zinc coating) zinc has the lower E^\circ (−0.76 V), so it oxidises in place of iron — a sacrificial coating that still protects a scratched surface
Cathodic protection blocks of Mg or Zn are bolted to pipelines and hulls and corrode instead of the steel
Painting, greasing, enamelling keeps out water and oxygen — a barrier, useless once broken
Alloying (stainless steel) chromium forms a thin adherent oxide film that seals the surface
Tin plating tin has a higher E^\circ; it protects only while the coat is intact, and makes rusting faster once scratched
The tin-can trap

A tin coating protects iron only as a physical barrier. Once the tin is scratched, the iron — lower in the series — becomes the anode and corrodes faster than it would unprotected. Zinc is the opposite: it keeps protecting even when scratched, because it is sacrificed.

Chapter summary

  • An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction; the anode is positive and the cathode negative, but oxidation is at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every cell.
  • Products of electrolysis follow preferential discharge: the ion with the higher E^\circ is reduced at the cathode; with inert electrodes in water, O₂ appears at the anode unless a concentrated halide gives Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂.
  • Faraday's first law: m = ZIt with Z = E/96\,500; second law: m_1/m_2 = E_1/E_2, and one faraday deposits one gram equivalent.
  • E^\circ is a reduction potential measured against the SHE (0.00 V; 1 M H⁺, 1 atm H₂, 298 K, Pt black); the calomel electrode is a portable secondary reference at about 0.24 V.
  • The electrochemical series gives reactivity, displacement, cell emf and electrolysis products; higher E^\circ gains electrons, lower E^\circ loses them.
  • E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}; positive means spontaneous; E^\circ is intensive, so doubling a half-reaction leaves it unchanged.
  • Nernst: E = E^\circ - (0.059/n)\log Q at 298 K; \Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ; at equilibrium E = 0 and E^\circ = (0.059/n)\log K.
  • Primary cells (dry cell 1.5 V, alkaline) cannot be recharged; secondary cells (lead–acid 2 V per cell, lithium-ion) can; fuel cells (H₂–O₂) run continuously and give only water.
  • Rusting is an electrochemical cell with iron as the anode; galvanising and cathodic protection work by sacrificing a metal with a lower E^\circ.

Model answer D1: galvanic cells, electrode potential and the Nernst equation (10 marks)

Introduction. A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. Oxidation occurs at the anode (negative) and reduction at the cathode (positive). In the Daniell cell:

  • Anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
  • Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
  • Cell notation: Zn | Zn²⁺(1 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu

The salt bridge (KCl or KNO₃ in agar) completes the circuit and keeps the solutions electrically neutral without mixing them.

Standard electrode potential. The potential of an electrode at 1\ \text{M}, 1\ \text{atm} and 25^{\circ}\text{C} measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, 0.00\ \text{V}). E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} (both as reduction potentials).

For the Daniell cell: 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10\ \text{V}.

Electrochemical series. A more negative E^{\circ} means a stronger reducing agent (Li, K, Zn), and a more positive E^{\circ} means a stronger oxidising agent (F₂, MnO₄⁻).

A metal displaces from solution another metal of higher E^{\circ} and one above hydrogen liberates H₂ from dilute acids.

Nernst equation. For aA + bB \to cC + dD at 25^{\circ}\text{C}:

E = E^{\circ} - \frac{0.0592}{n}\log Q

Link with thermodynamics. \Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}, \Delta G^{\circ} = -RT\ln K, so \log K = \dfrac{nE^{\circ}}{0.0592}. A reaction is spontaneous when E_{cell} > 0. At equilibrium E = 0 (a dead battery).

Quantity Formula
Free energy \Delta G = -nFE
Equilibrium constant \log K = nE^{\circ}/0.0592
Electrode potential E = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log\dfrac1{[M^{n+}]}

Numerical. For Zn | Zn²⁺(0.01 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M) | Cu: E = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.0592}{2}\log\dfrac{0.01}{1} = 1.10 + 0.059 = 1.16\ \text{V}.

Also \Delta G^{\circ} = -2\times96500\times1.10 = -212\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} and \log K = \dfrac{2\times1.10}{0.0592} = 37.2, so K \approx 10^{37}, a reaction that essentially goes to completion.

Conclusion. The Nernst equation links the cell potential to concentration, and E^{\circ} gives \Delta G^{\circ} and K.

Model answer D2: electrolysis and conductance (10 marks)

Introduction. Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. Oxidation occurs at the anode (positive) and reduction at the cathode (negative), the opposite polarity to a galvanic cell.

Faraday's laws.

  1. First law: the mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed: m = ZQ = ZIt.
  2. Second law: for the same charge, the masses of different substances deposited are proportional to their equivalent weights: \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{E_1}{E_2}.

So m = \dfrac{M\,I\,t}{nF}, with F = 96\,500\ \text{C mol}^{-1} (charge of one mole of electrons).

Products of electrolysis (the species with the higher reduction potential is discharged at the cathode, and the lower at the anode):

Electrolyte Cathode Anode
Molten NaCl Na Cl₂
Aqueous NaCl H₂ Cl₂
Aqueous CuSO₄ (Pt electrodes) Cu O₂
Aqueous CuSO₄ (Cu electrodes) Cu deposited Cu dissolves (refining)
Dilute H₂SO₄ H₂ O₂

Conductance. Resistance R = \rho l/A, conductivity \kappa = 1/\rho (S cm⁻¹), molar conductivity \Lambda_m = \dfrac{1000\,\kappa}{C}\ \text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1} (with C in mol L⁻¹).

For strong electrolytes \Lambda_m rises slowly on dilution (\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^{\circ} - A\sqrt C, Debye-Hückel-Onsager). For weak electrolytes it rises steeply near infinite dilution because ionisation increases.

Kohlrausch's law. At infinite dilution, each ion contributes independently: \Lambda_m^{\circ} = \lambda^{\circ}_+ + \lambda^{\circ}_-. This gives \Lambda^{\circ} for weak electrolytes, and the degree of ionisation \alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^{\circ}.

Batteries. Primary cells (dry cell), secondary cells (lead-acid with 2\ \text{V} per cell, Li-ion) and fuel cells (H₂-O₂, E^{\circ} = 1.23\ \text{V}).

Numerical.

  • 2\ \text{A} for 965\ \text{s} in CuSO₄: Q = 1930\ \text{C}, so 0.020\ \text{mol} of electrons deposit 0.010\ \text{mol} of Cu, 0.635\ \text{g}.
  • \Lambda^{\circ}(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = \Lambda^{\circ}(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda^{\circ}(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) - \Lambda^{\circ}(\text{NaCl}) = 426 + 91 - 126 = 391\ \text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}.
  • If a 0.1\ \text{M} acetic acid has \Lambda_m = 5.2, then \alpha = 5.2/391 = 1.3\%.

Conclusion. Faraday's laws fix the amount of substance for a given charge, and Kohlrausch's law gives the limiting conductivity of weak electrolytes.
